title: New insights into the genetic basis of Parkinson’s
summary: Researchers at Northwestern University used a genome-wide CRISPR interference screen and human genetic datasets to identify a 16-protein group termed Commander that affects lysosomal protein delivery. Loss-of-function variants in Commander genes may contribute to Parkinson's disease risk alongside known GBA1 variants. The findings highlight new potential drug targets and the possibility of combinatorial therapies targeting both Commander dysfunction and lysosomal GCase activity.

A new set of genes that contribute to Parkinson’s disease risk has been identified by researchers at Northwestern University.

Why do some individuals with Parkinson’s disease-associated genetic variants develop the disease while others do not? To address this question, the team investigated whether other genetic factors modify disease manifestation. Lysosomal dysfunction is a common feature of several neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson’s disease. The lysosome is the recycling center of the cell, responsible for breaking down waste material, old cell components and other unwanted substances.

Previous research showed that mutations in the GBA1 gene reduce lysosomal glucocerebrosidase activity, a key enzyme for lysosome function, and are linked to increased Parkinson’s risk. However, incomplete penetrance of GBA1 variants suggests additional genes influence whether disease develops. To search for such genes, the researchers performed a pooled genome-wide CRISPR interference screen to silence each protein-coding human gene in cells and identify those important for Parkinson’s pathogenesis.

The team used CRISPR interference, a gene-silencing technique that blocks gene expression without editing DNA. This method employs an inactive Cas9 protein, dCas9, guided by RNA to bind promoter regions and obstruct transcription, effectively reducing target gene expression.

Combining the experimental screen with analyses of genomes from the UK Biobank and AMP-PD, the researchers identified a group of 16 proteins they call Commander. Commander proteins play a previously unrecognized role in delivering specific proteins to the lysosome for recycling. In people with Parkinson’s, the team observed loss-of-function variants in Commander genes, supporting a model in which combinations of genetic factors contribute to disease manifestation.

The discovery suggests new therapeutic directions. If Commander dysfunction contributes to Parkinson’s, drugs targeting Commander could have broad potential for disorders linked to lysosomal dysfunction. Such therapies might also complement treatments aimed at increasing lysosomal glucocerebrosidase activity, enabling potential combinatorial approaches.

The authors note that further research is needed to determine how widely Commander proteins are involved in other neurodegenerative diseases associated with lysosomal dysfunction and to explore the feasibility of targeting Commander components pharmacologically.

A new set of genes that contribute to Parkinson’s disease risk has been identified.

Why is it that some individuals with Parkinson’s disease (PD)-associated genetic variants develop the disease, while others do not? Are there other genetic factors at play? Now, researchers atNorthwestern University(IL, USA) have identified a new set of genes implicated in developing PD, opening the door to new potential drug targets for treating this neurodegenerative disease.

Lysosomal dysfunction is a common feature of several neurodegenerative diseases, including PD. The lysosome is the recycling center of the cell, responsible for breaking down waste material, old cell components and other unwanted substances. Previous research has identified that mutations in theGBA1gene result in decreased lysosomal glucocerebrosidase (GCase) activity – a key enzyme for lysosome function – and are linked to increased PD risk. However, incomplete penetrance ofGBA1variants suggests that other genes are also involved in PD manifestation. To investigate the other genes potentially associated with PD, the team conducted a pooled genome-wide CRISPR screen.

Largest brain wiring diagram generated from grain-sized sample

A global team has constructed the most detailed wiring diagram of a mammalian brain to date.

The team used a modern technology calledCRISPR interferenceto examine the human genome. This gene-silencing technique works by blocking gene expression using an inactive form of the Cas9 protein, called dCas9, partnered with a guide RNA. The technique blocks gene expression without editing the DNA sequence; it can do this because the guide RNA can direct the dCas9 protein to bind – not cut – the promoter region of a target gene, which physically obstructs the RNA polymerase from transcribing the DNA.

“It also is possible to identify such genetic factors in susceptible individuals by studying tens of thousands of patients, which is challenging and costly,” explained corresponding author Dimitri Krainc. “Instead, we used a genome-wide CRISPR interference screen to silence each of the protein-coding human genes in cells and identified those important for PD pathogenesis.”

Examining genomes from theUK BiobankandAMP-PD, the team identified a group of 16 proteins – called Commander – that play a previously unrecognized role in delivering specific proteins to the lysosome for recycling. In people with PD, they observed loss-of-function variants in these Commander genes, demonstrating that a combination of genetic factors is implicated in PD manifestation and highlighting new potential drug targets.

“If Commander dysfunction is observed in these individuals, drugs that target Commander could hold broader therapeutic potential for treating disorders with lysosomal dysfunction,” Krainc concluded. “In this context, Commander-targeting drugs could also complement other PD treatments, such as therapies aiming to increase lysosomal GCase activity, as potential combinatorial therapy.”

Further research is needed to investigate the extent to which Commander proteins are involved in other lysosomal dysfunction-associated neurodegenerative diseases.

## Research Question

## Background

Lysosomal dysfunction is a common feature of several neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson’s disease. The lysosome is the recycling center of the cell, responsible for breaking down waste material, old cell components and other unwanted substances.

Previous research showed that mutations in the GBA1 gene reduce lysosomal glucocerebrosidase activity, a key enzyme for lysosome function, and are linked to increased Parkinson’s risk. However, incomplete penetrance of GBA1 variants suggests additional genes influence whether disease develops.

## Methods

To search for such genes, the researchers performed a pooled genome-wide CRISPR interference screen to silence each protein-coding human gene in cells and identify those important for Parkinson’s pathogenesis.

The team used CRISPR interference, a gene-silencing technique that blocks gene expression without editing DNA. This method employs an inactive Cas9 protein, dCas9, guided by RNA to bind promoter regions and obstruct transcription, effectively reducing target gene expression.

Combining the experimental screen with analyses of genomes from the UK Biobank and AMP-PD, the researchers searched for genetic modifiers of disease manifestation.

## Findings

The researchers identified a group of 16 proteins they call Commander. Commander proteins play a previously unrecognized role in delivering specific proteins to the lysosome for recycling. ## Implications

The discovery suggests new therapeutic directions. If Commander dysfunction contributes to Parkinson’s, drugs targeting Commander could have broad potential for disorders linked to lysosomal dysfunction.

Potential therapeutic strategies include:
- Drugs that directly target Commander components.
- Treatments aimed at increasing lysosomal glucocerebrosidase activity.
- Combinatorial approaches that combine Commander-targeted therapies with glucocerebrosidase-enhancing treatments.

The authors note that further research is needed to determine how widely Commander proteins are involved in other neurodegenerative diseases associated with lysosomal dysfunction and to explore the feasibility of targeting Commander components pharmacologically.
